source.title: Do Large Language Models Plan Answer Positions? Position Bias in Multiple-Choice Question Generation
source.authors: Xue-Mei Tang; Xu-Feng Duan; Zhen-Guang G. Cai

record.tranche_reason: The study probes question-stem representations for information about a later correct-answer position and intervenes on those representations to test their causal effect. This is a conceptual test of implicit planning, not the rhyme-generation method.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports answer-position distributions, identifier-removal effects, and balanced-prompting effects. Those findings are not rows here unless they directly measure future-position information or its causal manipulation. Probe baseline values and many plotted results are not numerically stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study probes question-stem hidden states for the correct-answer position of options generated later. It also steers those states at the penultimate stem token and measures A→B answer shifts in Llama-3.2-3B. That is a probe-plus-intervention test of internal look-ahead in a new task, MCQ generation, which bears on V5. It does not separate pre-caching from next-token side effects (V3). It does not decode future token identities (V2), and it involves no rhyme (V1, V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors add that steering 'can partially control positional preferences', and that position bias is intertwined with broader generation rather than an isolated mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses MLP probes and activation steering for MCQ answer positions, rather than rhyme-generation measurements or interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Intervention effects depend on injection position, layer, steering method, and scaling factor α. Penultimate-token steering is generally stronger than final-token steering; mean-difference steering is more effective and precise than classifier-based or random directions in the reported comparisons.
record.problems: The authors state that their probing and intervention results do not establish explicit symbolic planning. The intervention study uses one model and 200 samples selected with ground-truth answer A; intervention uncertainty estimates are not stated. Steering can alter question semantics, option space, coherence, or reasoning. The work is limited to controlled MCQ settings and deterministic decoding.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; fewer than 60 rows were extracted. General position-bias, identifier-removal, and balanced-prompting results were left out because they do not themselves measure future-position representations or their causal manipulation.

untested.parts: All of it: no rhyme, no verse, no frontier-model attribution.
Future token identity is not decoded; only a 4-way answer-position category is probed.
The study does not distinguish features computed for future use from next-token side effects, and it does not test breadcrumbs.
No rhyme planning in open models.
Planning horizon is not tested. Whether stem features such as topic or discipline (which correlate with position bias) explain probe accuracy is not controlled.

missing.what: Probing F1 under standard, standard without identifiers, and balanced without identifiers prompting. Average F1 drops without identifiers; under balanced w/o ID, Qwen-30B models maintain or improve F1 while smaller models show limited gains or slight drops.
Final-token trade-off: mean-difference at layer 6 gives about 16% target and about 6% off-target change. Classifier steering gives similar target shift but >10% off-target.
Case studies showing steering changes question semantics or replaces the task (semantic drift, task replacement, incoherence).

record.verdict_notes: The answer-position target is a categorical property of output many tokens later, so V2 is arguably adjacent but not met. Probe baseline values are figure-only. A possible confound is that stem content (discipline/topic) correlates with position bias, e.g. Mathematics favors A. That could make probe accuracy reflect question features rather than a plan, which the study does not rule out. Mean-difference vectors are built from groups by answer position, so steering may push content rather than position, consistent with the semantic-drift cases.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyme-word representations, rhyming verse, frontier models, and changing a rhyme candidate to alter the intervening line.
The probes predict a later answer-position category, not tokens several positions ahead.
The study does not distinguish features computed for later positions from information that is a side effect of next-token prediction, nor does it test the proposed breadcrumb mechanism directly.
No rhyme-planning test in open-weight models or use of open attribution-graph tools.
No multi-step reasoning, chess, or Sokoban tasks.
The study does not test planning horizon or whether local next-token features or heuristics explain the result.

rows.subject: all evaluated LLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Probe correct-answer-position information layer by layer.
rows.value: Figure only; text says predictive signals occur across a wide range of layers, not only final layers

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Add a mean-difference steering vector at the penultimate question-stem token to shift answer position from A toward B.
rows.baseline: Unintervened A-answer baseline; exact rate not stated
rows.note: The reported change is a minority of the selected A-answer samples, so the shift is causal but incomplete.
rows.check: Relink to V5. A maximum of 22.2% of A-answers shift to B, in one model with 200 selected samples.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Add random directions, norm-matched to the corresponding mean-difference direction, as a steering control.
rows.baseline: Unintervened A-answer baseline; exact rate not stated
rows.value: Plateaus at around 8–10%; at α = 400, about 40% of the mean-difference effect
rows.uncertainty: High variance at small α is stated; no numerical uncertainty given
rows.note: Random directions are a control and produce a smaller shift than the mean-difference direction.
rows.check: Control row: random norm-matched directions give about 8–10%. It serves as the baseline for r5 rather than a test of the effect. Injection position should be the penultimate token: Fig. 9 is layer 13, matching the 22.2% result.
